# C04 Dossier: Time-to-Power Fleet (P032 idea 5)

Date: 2026-10-18. Idea: hold a financed fleet of pre-built, multi-ratio 30-100 MVA substation transformers and sell, lease or option them for 8-16 week delivery. About 45 searches and fetches. Vendor, sponsored and aggregator sources are flagged. Inferences are marked.

## 1. Bottom line

**Verdict: weak, near-dead as framed. Big-and-defensible score 3/10.** The gate's "weak, ceiling $70M" is right on sales and generous on profit.

1. The "nobody holds stock" gap is false at the dealer layer. JCL, Giga, Maddox and Sunbelt Solomon already sell or rent stocked or fast units. What is genuinely empty is a multi-ratio 30-100 MVA fleet carrying stranded-project risk. The evidence suggests it is empty for physical and economic reasons.
2. $100M of revenue is reachable only as pass-through sales (gross profit about $11-14M) or with a $0.6-0.85B lease balance sheet that earns roughly its cost of capital only at near-full utilization (section 5).
3. The timing is bad. A fleet bought now takes delivery in 2028-29, when new OEM capacity lands and Rystad says prices and lead times have stopped rising.
4. Transformer delay is often not the binding constraint. Grid connection is.

## 2. Competitors: confirmed, refuted, added

**Gate competitors, all confirmed:**
- **Sunbelt Solomon.** 42 locations and 1,600+ staff. TJC is buying it from Trilantic (announced July 2026, terms undisclosed): https://www.pehub.com/tjc-to-acquire-electrical-power-firm-sunbelt-solomon-from-trilantic-north-america/ and https://www.cahill.com/news/firm-news/2026-07-24-cahill-private-credit-group-represents-financing-sources-in-tjc-acquisition-of-sunbelt-solomon. It advertises rental mobile substations to 230 kV and 50,000 kVA: https://sunbeltsolomon.com/mobile-substations/. A 2005 GE note says rentals above 20 MVA are usually pad-mounted units needing real site work, not trailers: https://www.renewableenergyworld.com/energy-business/ge-energy-introduces-new-mobile-transformer-for-rental-market/. No evidence of a leased 30-100 MVA fixed fleet. (A Prospeo "$27M revenue" estimate contradicts the headcount; ignore it.)
- **Maddox.** Stocks "thousands" of units, lets customers reserve manufacturing slots before final specs, and stores finished units until the site is ready (vendor/sponsored content): https://www.powermag.com/partner-content/beating-the-transformer-bottleneck-remanufacturing-build-to-stock-and-smart-procurement/. Its cited installs are 1-2 MVA, so it is the same product at distribution scale.
- **FluxCo.** "Transformer as a Service" lease and finance, vetted-manufacturer procurement, 10 to 500+ MVA: https://www.fluxco.com. $26M seed from Congruent and 8VC: https://fundraiseinsider.com/blog/fluxco-raises-26m-seed-for-ai-transformer-sourcing-platform/. No evidence it holds inventory.
- **Ayr Energy.** $25M raised, orders above $500M, Indian contract factories, modular designs that let customers change orders late: https://techcrunch.com/2026/04/15/this-energy-startups-bet-on-100-year-old-grid-tech-is-paying-off/. Advertises power transformers in 40-72 weeks against a 120-week 2024 average: https://www.ayr.energy. Late-change modularity attacks the same "cannot commit" pain without owning stock.
- **Grid Assurance.** Cost-based, five-year subscriptions for transmission-owner emergency spares. FERC allowed single-issue ratemaking for subscribers: https://www.troutmanenergyreport.com/2016/04/ferc-issues-regulatory-findings-on-subscription-service-for-spare-transmission-equipment/. It is a different job (spares, not new load).

**Added by this research:**
- **JCL Energy.** "One of the largest independently held inventories of padmount and substation transformers," power class to 345 kV, same-week shipment, bridge-power rentals, blanket POs for multi-year programs. No unit counts: https://www.jcl.energy/projects/markets/utilities
- **Giga Energy.** Sells 69-138 kV substation transformers to 100 MVA, "in-stock and custom," made-to-order "as fast as 26 weeks," a hyperscaler testimonial of 7 weeks (vendor claims): https://gigaenergy.com/substation-transformers. Aggregator funding data conflict ($3.6M to about $30M): https://www.premieralts.com/companies/giga-energy/funding-history
- **Middleman supply.** Bolt Electrical says a standard substation transformer ships 12-14 months after drawing approval for 12-15% above factory cost (the article calls it hard to validate): https://powermag.com/transformers-in-2026-shortage-scramble-or-self-inflicted-crisis/
- **Quanta Services.** $500-700M toward power-transformer manufacturing (secondary): https://transformer-technology.com/quanta-services-reports-record-revenue-guidance-highlights-transformer-investment/
- **Utility pools.** North Carolina's co-op pool has eight mobile substations (5-30 MVA, 16 members, dues by capacity share): https://www.cooperative.com/remagazine/articles/Pages/Tech-Insights-Power-Pool.aspx
- **Hyperscalers buy direct.** One confidential hyperscaler's substations use owner-furnished 120-150 MVA Siemens units at 161 kV: https://jedunn.com/projects/confidential-data-center-substation/. Note the size sits above the idea's 30-100 MVA window.
- **Substitutes.** Solid-state transformer startups (Heron $140M Series B; DG Matrix $60M): https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/heron-power-raises-140m-in-series-b-funding-to-support-build-out-of-40gw-us-manufacturing-facility/. Developers also refurbish old units and add on-site generation: https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-11/us-power-transformer-buyers-scramble-imports-factory-slots

**Correction to the idea:** the Datacentres.com article it cites for Dominion, AEP Ohio and Consumers collateral contains none of that. It has only the anonymous colo quote ("ordering transformers before we've signed the interconnection agreement") and a £3M deposit example: https://www.datacentres.com/news/36-month-lead-times-turn-transformer-shortage-into-data-centre-site-selection-ki-slot3-2026-08-07. Treat the Dominion "$1.5M per MW" figure as unverified; I could not confirm it.

## 3. Bottom-up market and the payer

**Sourced anchors.**
- In 2019 US demand for transformers above 60 MVA was about 750 units, 82% imported, and DOE expected about 900 a year by 2027: https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2024-10/EXEC-2022-001242%20-%20Large%20Power%20Transformer%20Resilience%20Report%207-10-24.pdf
- Wood Mackenzie says substation power transformer demand is up 116% since 2019 (Reuters): https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-11/us-power-transformer-buyers-scramble-imports-factory-slots
- Vendor estimates put large US units at $2.1B in 2025: https://www.kenresearch.com/industry-reports/united-states-large-power-transformer-market. Mordor Intelligence puts all US power transformers at $4.49B (seen only in a search summary; URL not verified).
- Price benchmark: recent European awards for 50-100 MVA run $30-35k per MVA, so about $1.5-1.75M at 50 MVA, $2.5-2.9M at 84 MVA, $3.0-3.5M at 100 MVA: https://powerpeakdigest.com/global-transformer-supply-constraints-ease-rystad/
- Dominion keeps filing 84 MVA units for Loudoun substations: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/teac/2026/20260106/20260106-item-07---dom-supplemental-projects.pdf. This shows convergence inside one utility, not across utilities.

**Inference.** The 30-100 MVA slice is perhaps $1.5-3B a year, about 800-1,600 units. No source splits it. $100M of sales is 3-7% of it. Average unit price is nearer $2M than the idea's $3M, so $100M needs about 50 units, not 35.

**Who signs.** A developer VP Power or CFO, or a utility chief engineer or supply-chain VP once an electric service agreement is signed. The fleet's marginal customer is the one who cannot get a direct OEM slot, which means mid-size developers and neoclouds. Only about 12% of requested data-center load is firm and 17% likely (via Bloomberg; the shares sum to 29% against a stated 28%): https://capacityglobal.com/news/wood-mackenzie-us-grid-operators-set-to-serve-28pc-of-data/. Inference: buyers asking for an unsigned-project reservation skew toward the speculative 72%, and the credit-worthy 12% already hold OEM frames.

## 4. Demand and willingness to pay

**For:**
- Developers "pay significant premiums or buy production slots well in advance, sometimes before a specific project exists" (Burns & McDonnell in Reuters): https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-11/us-power-transformer-buyers-scramble-imports-factory-slots
- Roseville moved from buying one year ahead to three, and now buys for projects five years out. Some buyers prepay for earlier slots: https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-07-09/us-power-companies-scramble-secure-equipment-surging-data-center
- A Utah city's order is "two years out" on 30/30/40 payment milestones (order, drawing approval, shipment): https://sanpetemessenger.com/mt-pleasant-approves-major-transformer-purchase-delays-a-fire-billing-ordinance/
- A Michigan city chose Virginia Transformer ($1.32M, up to 1.5 years) over Niagara ($1.28M, 3.5-5 years), paying 3.4% more to save 2-3.5 years: https://transformer-technology.com/harbor-springs-advances-6-million-electrical-substation-project-with-transformer-purchase-transformer-technology-news/

**Against:**
- No RFP, tender or contract for a leased or stocked 30-100 MVA fleet turned up. The nearest are the co-op pool above and sub-50 MVA rentals.
- The only sourced markup for speed is Bolt's 12-15% over factory cost for 12-14 months, not 8-16 weeks.
- Wesco's CEO calls power availability the main constraint (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/08/03/wesco-wcc-q2-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Its slide shows "3-5 Years Time to Power" against a 1-2 year build: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000929008/000092900826000012/wcc-1q2026slides.htm. A stocked transformer does not shorten a 3-5 year interconnection.
- Rules now penalize speculation. AEP Ohio requires 85% of subscribed demand for up to 12 years plus exit fees: https://www.powermag.com/regulator-approves-aep-ohios-landmark-data-center-tariff/. Virginia moves to 14-year contracts and collateral in January 2027: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/715957/000119312526115192/dei-ars-12312025.pdf. Texas SB 6 requires site control and duplicate-request disclosure: https://www.utilitydive.com/news/efforts-to-curb-data-center-speculation-gain-ground-across-the-us/830495/. Inference: this removes the weakest demand and leaves buyers who can order direct.

## 5. Unit economics and capital

**Sale route.** 35-50 units for about $100M at a 12-15% markup is about $11-14M gross profit (my arithmetic on Bolt's markup). That is a dealer's spread, before carrying cost.

**Lease route.** Willis Lease reports a lease-rate factor of about 1.04% a month, roughly 12.5% a year, on aircraft engines: https://allmind.ai/earnings/event/bt_WLFC_2025_Q3. That matches the idea's 12-15%, but engines have deep lessee pools and global resale. No transformer lease comp exists; FluxCo and Sunbelt Solomon do not publish rates.

My illustration (assumptions: 280 units at $2.5M = $700M; 70% debt at 7.5%; 2.5% depreciation on DOE's 40-year life; 2% storage, insurance and logistics):

| Utilization | Revenue at 12.5% | Costs | Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 70% | $61M | $68M | negative |
| 100% | $88M | $68M | $20M |

The $20M roughly equals a 10% return on the $210M of equity. Break-even is about 78% utilization, and earning a 10% equity return needs about 100%.

**Capital.** Startups in this niche have raised tens of millions (Ayr $25M, FluxCo $26M), against $0.6-0.85B for the fleet. OEMs allocate slots on forecast certainty, and the DOE report says plant build-out takes 1-3 years, so a new buyer without frames queues behind hyperscalers. Buyers normally fund the OEM in stages (the 30/30/40 terms above); a fleet must front all of it. The workable form is a floorplan-financed dealer or lessor, which is what JCL, Maddox and Sunbelt Solomon already are. Sunbelt Solomon (a 2019 merger plus add-ons, now a private-credit-financed PE sale) shows the route exists but is a multi-year roll-up: https://www.privsource.com/acquisitions/deal/zqSlxv

## 6. Legal, regulatory and liability

- **EO 14420 (Aug 26, 2026).** Reaches foreign-produced bulk-power equipment of 69 kV and up from "covered foreign entities" (ITAR 126.1-type countries; China is the main supplier). DOE rules are due in 120 days (about Dec 24), and installed equipment can be isolated or removed: https://www.morganlewis.com/blogs/powerandpipes/2026/08/bulk-power-system-executive-order-adds-a-new-grid-supply-chain-compliance-layer. Korea, India and Mexico are not named, so allied-origin sourcing is lawful. The risk is sub-tier provenance on speculative stock (Chinese bushings or controllers in a Korean unit) if DOE tightens definitions. DOE's comment window closed Oct 9 (per the gate: https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/doe-rfi-bulk-power-system-eo.html). Whether "bulk power" reaches data-center loads is unclear: https://www.woodmac.com/press-releases/us-executive-order-banning-chinese-bulk-power-equipment-set-to-worsen-critical-transformer-shortage/. The 2020 predecessor order was suspended and never reinstated.
- **Tariffs.** A 50% duty on steel and aluminum content of transformers since Aug 2025 (https://tedmag.com/trump-administration-increases-tariffs-on-certain-transformers/). I could not confirm the April 2026 restructuring. Inventory is exposed to repricing in either direction.
- **Efficiency standards.** DOE's 2024 rule covers distribution transformers and is under reconsideration: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-04-22/html/2024-07480.htm. I found no federal efficiency standard for the 30-100 MVA class; verify the scope boundary.
- **Spec acceptance (the real legal-technical risk).** DOE: impedance is "a particularly difficult parameter to standardize," and large units are "very site-specific." Flexible designs cost more and one ran about 12% heavier. ABB's modular approach is "relatively high-cost": the DOE report above. DHS/EPRI's flexible spare replaces over 90% of 345/138 kV units, but voltage and MVA must match, impedance must be close, and some transmission owners vetoed a common design: https://dhs.gov/sites/default/files/publications/RecX%20-%20Emergency%20Spare%20Transformer%20Strategy-508.pdf. One utility's flexible spare is expected to last 5-10 years, not 40. Each (high side, low side, MVA, impedance, vector group) combination is a separate SKU, so "multi-ratio" does not collapse the fleet to a few designs.
- **Procurement law.** Public utilities bid competitively (the two Michigan bids above), so selling to them from a fleet needs a qualifying bid.
- **Liability.** The fleet seller inherits warranty and early-failure risk (HSB: design and manufacturing issues are the second-leading failure cause, often at energization, per the Maddox article). Idle oil-filled units need storage maintenance per DOE. Whether a stored spare is "operational equipment" under EPA SPCC rules is unconfirmed: https://www.epa.gov/node/222171. Hoarding optics: the DPA determination calls capacity "dangerously limited"; I found no 2026 use of DPA anti-hoarding or priority-rating authority on grid equipment: https://www.enr.com/articles/62887-trump-taps-defense-production-act-to-address-grid-equipment-energy-project-bottlenecks

## 7. Is the why-now real?

**Real:**
- Power-transformer lead times of 128 weeks and GSUs of 144 weeks (Wood Mackenzie Q2 2025): https://powermag.com/transformers-in-2026-shortage-scramble-or-self-inflicted-crisis/. GSU lead times exceeded 160 weeks by Q1 2026 (Reuters link above).
- 2025 deficits of 30% (power) and 10% (distribution): https://www.pv-magazine.com/2025/08/15/us-transformer-supply-may-fall-sharply-in-2025-says-wood-mackenzie/
- In 2025 Mexico, China, South Korea and Europe supplied 76% of US imports of 10-100 MVA units, so a China cut-off bites in this class (Rystad link above). Goldman data say China supplies only about 4% of US demand, which conflicts with Wood Mackenzie's "virtually all bulk-power imports": https://greentechlead.com/power/us-ban-on-chinese-power-equipment-threatens-22-billion-import-market-as-transformer-shortage-deepens-55085

**Used up or fading:**
- Wood Mackenzie's 2026 shortage estimate is 15% for power transformers (30% in 2025) and 8% for substations (woodmac link above).
- Rystad (June 2026): growth in prices and lead times has "largely stalled," peak lead times could ease within 12 months, and nearly 200 GVA of capacity arrives in 2026, with the US taking 35-40% of additions through 2028 (powerpeakdigest link).
- New US plants: Siemens Charlotte early 2027, Eaton 2027, Hitachi Virginia 2028 (Power link above).
- Correlated downside: in 2025 Microsoft reportedly walked away from about 2 GW of projects (TD Cowen): https://w.media/microsoft-cancels-2gw-data-center-projects-in-us-and-europe/. The idea's "portfolio effect" fails when every lessee's demand falls together.

Inference: the window for a fleet is roughly 2027-29, and slots ordered today deliver at its end.

## 8. Upside-case assumptions tested

| Assumption | Finding |
|---|---|
| 35 units at $3M = $105M | $3M is a 100 MVA price. The class midpoint is nearer $2M, so about 50 units. Gross profit about $11-14M. |
| Lease at 12-15% of cost | Plausible by aircraft analogy (12.5%). No transformer comp. Needs about 100% utilization to earn its equity cost. |
| "About 80% of substation units are the same few designs" | Unsourced. DOE says site-specific with impedance the hardest parameter. Only intra-utility convergence (Dominion 84 MVA). |
| 280 data-center units a year | Rests on 24 to 110 GW by 2030. If only the 28% firm/likely share applies, it is about 80 (inference). Hyperscale buys direct, and at least one hyperscaler uses 120-150 MVA units. |
| 8-16 week delivery | Beyond any sourced made-to-order claim (Giga 26 weeks; Ayr 40-72 weeks). Equals stock sales. |
| Fleet turnover of 100-140 units a year is 15-25% of flow | No sourced denominator. On my 800-1,600 estimate it is 6-18% of flow (inference), so share is less heroic than claimed, but only if that sizing holds. |
| EO makes allied-origin stock scarce | Real but modest. Allied supply is expanding fast. |

## 9. Verdict and what would change it

The only version that clears $100M revenue is a balance-sheet dealer/lessor roll-up. The lessons file accepts a balance sheet as a scalable asset, but the spread here is thin and cyclical (about 10-13% gross on resale; roughly cost of capital on lease). Narrowing to one voltage class would drop it under $25M, which the rules forbid as a rescue. **Call it dead as a startup, weak as a financing play.**

It revives only if all hold: (a) three utilities sign off one multi-ratio spec in writing; (b) an OEM commits slots at a fixed price with a buy-back or resale floor; (c) a lender prices the fleet above 70% loan-to-value; (d) DOE's December rules or a federal purchase commitment make stocked allied-origin units a mandated category.

**Gaps.** No sourced US count of 10-100 MVA units. No transformer lease-rate comp. No Sunbelt Solomon revenue. Wood Mackenzie primary reports were unavailable (press and secondary only). Dominion's per-MW collateral is unconfirmed.

# C03 dossier: Neutral HCBS operating system for D-SNP-aligned Medicaid plans (pool P061, idea 5)

Researched 2026-10-18. Tags: (S) read in a source this session, (A) my arithmetic or assumption, (U) unverified. Where a page would not load, I say the figure came through a search summary. About 55 searches, fetches and filing pulls.

## 1. Bottom line

Wounded, and the upside case does not hold. The category is real and the buyer has a budget line: CareBridge reached 115,000 patients and a reported $2.6B of 2023 revenue in about four years and was bought for a reported $2.7B. But four things weaken the pick.

1. **The "neutral vacuum" is unproven, and the sharpened wedge is already occupied.** I found no rival plan leaving CareBridge. Elevance now says CareBridge supports "nearly 200,000 patients" and moved into D-SNPs in 2025.
2. **The gate missed independent competitors** that sell to the same buyer: CareCentrix, Cityblock plus Homeward, and HHAeXchange's payer tools.
3. **The 5% net margin behind the 67-90k member path is at the top of observed analogs** (3.4% for Carelon Services, 5-8% for Evolent).
4. **The "savings only" pilot cannot reach $100M** (section 3).

Revenue test: $100M of gross premium needs only about 4,000 fully capitated members, so the revenue rule is not binding. Profit is what matters, and $100M of profit needs about 67,000 at-risk members, or 3.6% of all managed-LTSS users (A). My read: the gate's $20M median is fair, and the $100M upside is under 10% likely (judgment). The credible large outcome is a strategic sale to a plan, not a standalone $100M-profit company.

## 2. Competitors: confirmed, refuted, new

| Player | Verdict vs gate | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| CareBridge / Carelon (Elevance) | Confirmed, and bigger than the gate said | FY2025 10-K: $1,827M goodwill plus $305M finite-lived intangibles (S, [10-K Note 3](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1156039/000115603926000013/elv-20251231.htm)). Elevance's page: "nearly 200,000 patients across 16 states and Washington, D.C.", D-SNP 24/7 model added in 2025, company-reported 12% fewer admissions, 13% fewer ED visits and 10-15% MLR improvement for D-SNP patients, no methods given ([Elevance](https://www.elevancehealth.com/our-approach-to-health/care-provider-partnership/delivering-whole-person-care-right-at-home)). CareBridge's own site lists 18 states plus DC ([CareBridge](https://www.carebridgehealth.com/who-we-serve)); the counts conflict. Q2 2026 10-Q credits "expansion of CareBridge" ([10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001156039/000115603926000060/elv-20260630.htm)). |
| Plans' in-house LTSS teams | Confirmed, strong | Centene alone: 338K+ LTSS members in 15 states (Jan 2025), local care-management teams, area-agency and independent-living partnerships ([Centene](https://www.centene.com/content/dam/centenedotcom/documents/ltss-one-pager.pdf)). |
| HHAeXchange | Confirmed, and more overlap than the idea admits | Payer products: provider network management, program-integrity analytics, caregiver "change in condition" insights, BI dashboards, claims validation; 485M visits, $38B payments, 2.5M members ([MCO page](https://www.hhaexchange.com/solutions/mco)). 180+ MCOs, 32,000 providers, 30 state programs; Care Insights since Feb 2022 ([HHAX](https://www.hhaexchange.com/press-releases/hhaexchange-launches-care-insights-solution-to-help-payers-reduce-risk)). I found no risk-taking product. |
| CareCentrix | **New. Refutes "no independent risk-bearing manager found."** | LTSS program for plans with analytics, remote monitoring and transitions of care ([CareCentrix](https://go.carecentrix.com/LTSS)); a search summary describes a Medicaid model of value-based contracts and guaranteed savings, in Medicaid since 2020. Carved out of Walgreens as a standalone private company in Aug 2025 ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/08/sycamore-acquires-walgreens-carecentix-goes-it-alone/)); sources conflict on whether Sycamore or the Pessina family holds it. Medicaid revenue not disclosed. |
| Cityblock + Homeward | **New** | All-stock deal plus $116M Series E, Aug 21 2026: about 200K members, about $2.2B annualized revenue, up 77% ([HLTH](https://hlth.com/insights/news/cityblock-acquires-homeward-and-raises-116m-to-expand-integrated-urban-rural-care)). Centene's fourth regional deal with it (Meridian Illinois, Jan 2026, 10,000 Medicaid members; earlier NY, OH, FL) ([HCFN](https://www.healthcarefinancenews.com/news/cityblock-health-and-meridian-health-plan-illinois-partner-medicaid)). Partial overlap (care delivery, not HCBS operations). |
| Papa | Low overlap | 40+ plans, companionship, Medicare Advantage focus; Medicaid not mentioned (search summary). |
| Optum | Adjacent (U) | Closed the $3.3B Amedisys deal in Aug 2025, after LHC ([Healthcare Dive](https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/unitedhealth-closes-amedisys-buy-doj/757742/)). Whether Optum sells Medicaid HCBS management to rivals: not found. |

Free substitutes: state EVV aggregators, plan care coordinators, and the free CareBridge EVV that Iowa lets providers use (Iowa HHS materials, via search summary). No new venture-funded HCBS-specific manager found besides Cityblock.

## 3. Market: bottom-up

- **Managed-LTSS users, July 2024 (S):** 1,426,227 in comprehensive managed care plus 429,894 in MLTSS-only plans = 1,856,121 ([CMS dataset via API](https://data.medicaid.gov/api/1/datastore/query/5394bcab-c748-5e4b-af07-b5bf77ed3aa3/0)). State-reported, includes nursing-facility users, Medicaid-only and duals; CMS warns definitions differ.
- **Concentration (S):** NY 346,892 (mostly NY MLTC-only plans), CA 312,162, TX 152,030, FL 139,572, PA 131,370 = 1,082,026, or 58%. Only 25 states report any.
- **Spend per user (S/A):** MACPAC FY2023: 6.6M LTSS users, $329.0B (38.7% of $850.1B benefit spending), about $49.8k each across all services ([MACPAC](https://www.macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/EXHIBIT-20.-Distribution-of-Medicaid-Enrollment-and-Benefit-Spending-by-Users-and-Non-Users-of-Long-Term-Services-and-Supports-FY-2023.pdf)). The idea's $30k of managed HCBS spend per member is plausible.
- **Aligned D-SNP pool (S):** 6,084,997 D-SNP enrollees, of which 1,975,250 HIDE and 743,683 FIDE, so 2,718,933 integrated ([HMA](https://www.healthmanagement.com/blog/in-focus/hma-resource-provides-key-insights-about-the-evolving-medicare-medicaid-integration-landscape/)). The 2027 rule limits certain D-SNPs to members of an affiliated Medicaid plan. HCBS use among them: not found. If 15-25% use HCBS (U), the aligned HCBS pool is 0.4-0.7M, and 67k members is 10-16% of it (A).
- **Reachable payers (A/U):** about 6-10 non-Elevance parents have more than 50k LTSS lives (Centene, UHC, Molina, Humana, CVS/Aetna, AmeriHealth Caritas, large Blues), plus NY local plans. Not sourced as a count.
- **Revenue per contract (A):** a 10,000-member regional deal (Cityblock-Meridian size) at $30k is $300M of managed spend, or $9-15M of profit at 3-5%. A 5,000-member pilot is $4.5-7.5M. $100M needs 7-11 such deals.
- **Three ways to count $100M (A):**
  - Gross premium at about $25k per capitated member: about 4,000 members. Profit is $3-8M.
  - Net margin at 3% / 5% / 8% of $30k: about 111k / 67k / 42k members.
  - Shared savings only: 20% of 5-10% savings is $300-600 per member, so 167k-333k members, or 9-18% of all managed-LTSS users. **Dead as a standalone path.**

## 4. Demand and willingness to pay

- **Strong precedent (S):** CareBridge's $140M 2022 round was led by Oak HC/FT with Anthem, Optum Ventures, CVS Ventures and HLM (for Centene). Its CEO said those plans oversee about 60% of HCBS members. It took risk "based on a member's historic spending" and employed no home workers ([BHB](https://bhbusiness.com/2022/06/16/how-carebridge-won-over-investors-mcos-in-140m-funding-round/)). It grew from about 25k to about 115k patients in about a year ([HCI](https://www.hcinnovationgroup.com/policy-value-based-care/medicare-medicaid/news/53071689/medicaid-focused-carebridge-tops-inc-magazines-fastest-growing-list)).
- **Rivals did buy from it (S):** a 2023 Iowa deck says CareBridge was a subcontractor of all three Iowa plans: Amerigroup (Elevance), Iowa Total Care (Centene) and Molina ([Iowa HHS](https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/535/download)). Iowa also asked to pause CareBridge's member outreach because of confusion. Iowa's 2026 EVV materials still show all plans using CareBridge EVV (search summary; Iowa's EVV model may be partly state-driven).
- **Rivals buy from neutral vendors (S):** Centene's four Cityblock deals. The one visible first-contract size is 10,000 lives, not 70,000.
- **No evidence of the neutral demand itself (negative finding):** I found no RFP, posted contract, plan statement or press report from Centene, UHC, Molina, Humana or CVS seeking an HCBS manager free of Elevance, and none of a plan leaving CareBridge since the Dec 2024 close. Elevance's CEO said it would keep serving all customers (Fierce, via search summary). Whether CareBridge still serves rivals after the close: not verifiable.
- **No mandate forces vendor spend (S):** EVV is done. The 80/20 pass-through stays on the books for July 2030 ([LeadingAge](https://leadingage.org/serialpost/cms-significant-medicaid-rules-addressing-access-and-quality/)). The 2027 D-SNP alignment rules raise plan interest in integrated management, but they do not require a vendor.

## 5. Unit-economics analogs

- **Carelon Services segment (S, [10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1156039/000115603926000013/elv-20251231.htm)):** 2025 revenue $28,316M, operating gain $960M = 3.4%. 2024: $17,961M and $717M = 4.0%. Premiums (risk contracts) rose from $1,679M (2023) to $2,630M to $6,315M (2025). About 75% of revenue is affiliated ($21,175M). The segment recognizes risk revenue gross: a PMPM premium with responsibility for claims cost ([10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001156039/000115603926000060/elv-20260630.htm)).
- **Evolent (neutral risk-bearing platform, via search summary of the [8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1628908/000162890826000014/a2025q4exhibit991.htm)):** 2025 revenue $1,876M, adjusted EBITDA $151M (8.1%), $398M Q4 goodwill impairment. 2026 guidance $110-140M EBITDA on $2.4-2.6B, about 5%.
- **CareBridge exit (S/A):** about 1.0x reported 2023 revenue. If its margin resembled the two analogs (3-8%), the price is roughly 13-35x operating profit, which prices growth, not current earnings (A).
- **Revenue per member differs by model (S/A):** CareBridge about $22.6k ($2.6B over 115k, a mixed definition); Cityblock about $11k ($2.2B over 200k).
- **Implication:** 5% of $30k is a good-year profit rate, not a fee. The gate's $1,100-1,500 per member holds only for a full-risk book, which carries volatility and capital needs (sections 6 and 7).

## 6. Capital needs

- CareBridge raised $180M of equity across two rounds before its exit ([BHB](https://bhbusiness.com/2022/06/16/how-carebridge-won-over-investors-mcos-in-140m-funding-round/)). It had about 500 employees at the deal ([Fierce](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/finance/elevance-health-scoop-value-based-care-company-carebridge), via search summary).
- My estimate for a non-anchored entrant: $100-200M to reach about 30-50k members (A). That covers clinical and EVV-data build, plus risk reserves, stop-loss and any surety or solvency capital a state requires. Plans pay capitation before providers are paid, so working capital is a smaller issue than variance.
- **Structural problem (A):** the sharpened design funds the vendor with 2-3 plans' co-investment. In 2022 Anthem was an investor; in 2024 Elevance was the buyer. Plan co-investors get first look at an exit, and a plan seat on the governance board is the opposite of neutrality.

## 7. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **Plan stays on the hook (S):** under [42 CFR 438.230](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/438.230), a plan keeps ultimate responsibility, and delegation must be revocable. State, CMS and OIG get audit rights for 10 years. Plans will price that into contracts and favor vendors they can fire or absorb.
- **Licensure when taking capitated risk (S, examples only):** Arkansas treats a licensed risk-based provider organization as an insurer ([Ark. Rule 117](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/arkansas/054-00-17-Ark-Code-R-002)). California's Knox-Keene scope was widened in 2019. Delaware certifies risk-bearing entities. CMS counts entities paid a fixed periodic amount as sub-capitated ([CMS](https://www.medicaid.gov/tmsis/dataguide/t-msis-coding-blog/cms-technical-instructions-reporting-sub-capitation-payments-and-encounters-associated-with-sub-capitation-payments-from-managed-care-plans/)). I found no HCBS-specific rule, so each state is a separate licensing check.
- **Hours and authorization liability (S/U):** Arkansas's ARChoices algorithm cut home-care hours; a court found notice failures in 2018, and the vendor's tool mishandled diabetes and cerebral palsy ([Arkansas Online](https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2018/may/24/dhs-found-in-contempt-over-rule-changes-1/); vendor-liability ruling not found). *Lokken v. UnitedHealth* over nH Predict is in discovery (secondary source). If the product steers hours or networks, due-process and fair-hearing exposure falls on the plan and lands on the vendor by indemnity.
- **Savings capture (S):** CHCS says HCBS quality savings tend to accrue to Medicare ([CHCS](https://www.chcs.org/early-state-efforts-to-advance-value-in-medicaid-managed-long-term-services-and-supports-programs/)). That is why FIDE/HIDE alignment is the right buyer, and also why the buyer pool is small. A California budget document also warns that capitation rebasing passes plan savings back to the state in later years (undated; U).
- **Evidence base:** the only outcome numbers I found for this model are Elevance's, with no methods.

## 8. Is the why-now real?

- **Real and live:** plan Medicaid margins are squeezed. Molina guides a 92.6% medical cost ratio and calls 2026 a "trough year" for Medicaid margins ([S&P](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/articles/2026/8/us-health-insurers-raise-outlooks-despite-q2-cost-rises-shifting-membership-105000456)). H.R.1 state-directed-payment cuts start Jan 1, 2028, and 15 states plan new cost containment in FY2026 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/states-management-of-medicaid-home-care-spending-ahead-of-h-r-1-effects/)). Integrated D-SNP alignment is in force: 22 states have applicable integrated plans, up from 14.
- **Half-used:** the Elevance purchase closed 22 months ago and nothing I found shows rivals defecting. The shock that was meant to open the neutral slot has not visibly produced demand. Tight margins also cut vendor budgets and push plans to in-source or use free HHAX tools.
- **Already occupied:** Elevance extended CareBridge to D-SNPs in 2025, the sharpened wedge.

## 9. Upside-case assumptions, tested

| Assumption | Finding | Holds? |
|---|---|---|
| 70-90k at-risk members by year 6 | CareBridge took about four years to reach 115k with four plan-investors and a $180M raise. Neutral entrants today start with 5-10k-life contracts, so this needs 7-11 deals. | Top-decile only |
| About 5% net margin ($1,100-1,500 per member) | Carelon Services 3.4%, Evolent 5-8%, falling to about 5% in 2026. A fee model earns $300-600. | Optimistic |
| 2-3 non-Elevance plans co-invest for volume | 2022 precedent exists. But the co-investor-then-acquirer pattern (Anthem) undermines neutrality, and no plan has shown interest. | Unproven |
| Rivals will not trust a competitor's subsidiary | Iowa shows rivals did use CareBridge; no defections found; Centene uses neutral Cityblock. | Weak or refuted |
| D-SNP alignment makes savings capturable | True in principle (2027 rules, 2.7M integrated members), but Elevance entered first and HCBS use among aligned members is unquantified. | Plausible, contested |
| Pool is big enough | 1.86M managed-LTSS users, 58% in five states, NY mostly local plans. Aligned HCBS pool maybe 0.4-0.7M (U). | Marginal |
| Defensible vs. incumbents | CareBridge, CareCentrix, Cityblock and HHAX already sell to the buyer; plans like Centene have 338K in-house LTSS lives. | Contested |

## 10. Kill tests and gaps

- **Three plan calls (the idea's own test):** ask Centene, UHC and Molina LTSS leads whether they would move at-risk HCBS lives from CareBridge or in-house to a neutral vendor, at what share, and on what terms (savings only or delegated risk).
- **Pull CareBridge subcontractor lists** from state Medicaid sites (Iowa, Tennessee, Texas, Ohio, Arizona) to see whether non-Elevance plans still use it.
- **Get CareCentrix Medicaid LTSS terms and size.** This is the closest independent comparable and I could not find its numbers.
- **HCBS use among FIDE/HIDE members:** not found; it decides the pool size.
- **Not found:** plan-to-vendor fee benchmarks; sales cycle length for a neutral entrant; any independent outcome study of CareBridge; whether CareBridge keeps contracts with Centene, UHC, Molina, Humana or CVS after the close.
- **Source caveats:** the $2.6B and $2.7B figures are press-reported (one outlet cites $4B+ revenue). The CMS counts are state-reported. Some items came only through search summaries: CareCentrix's guaranteed-savings model, Evolent's results, and the Papa, Optum, Iowa-EVV and Fierce items.

**Call:** do not pursue as a standalone $100M-profit company. If pursued at all, test as a regional, contract-anchored risk manager built to be acquired. Say plainly that the defensible version is smaller than the pitch.

# C02 dossier: P061 "Fiscal-intermediary consolidator with a payroll-certainty SLA"

Research date 2026-10-18. Marks: (A) my arithmetic or assumption; † = read only in a search-result summary, page not opened; Louisiana is taken from the gate file because the memo returned 403.

## Verdict

The spend is real, mandated and signed by a state. But the fee is only about 2% of program spend, the only public cost data I found (state-reviewed Wisconsin summaries) shows the sector losing money at about 28,000 participants, the one $100M-class contract (New York) is locked until about 2030 and under federal attack, recent rebids went to multi-state incumbents, and private equity is already rolling up the same assets. I rate this **weak-to-moderate, not "strong"**. The gate's $20M median revenue is plausible. Profit at that size is near zero. The $110M upside needs conditions that do not exist today.

## 1. Industry metrics (Step 0)

What this industry runs on: admin fee per participant per month (PMPM), participants under contract, operating cost per participant-month, contract term and rebid cycle, working-capital and reserve rules, and past-performance eligibility.

## 2. Market: bottom-up

- **Pool.** The 2023 inventory counted 1,520,267 self-directing people and says California is 48% of them ([NCI deck](https://nci-ad.org/images/uploads/SarahTaubWebSeries_1.24_.25_.pdf)). California's IHSS (800,000+ recipients) runs on state and county payroll, not FMS vendors ([CHCF](https://www.chcf.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/InHomeSupportiveServicesIntegrationManagedCare.pdf)†). So at most about 790,000 people are outside California (A); the gate's 0.7-1.0M is at or above that ceiling. New York's CDPAP is about 250,000 of them ([Lawyer Monthly](https://www.lawyer-monthly.com/2026/06/justice-department-sues-ppl-new-york-medicaid-fraud/)). That leaves **about 540,000 outside CA and NY (A)**, an upper bound because it includes veteran-directed and non-FMS programs.
- **Price points.**
  - New York bid: $68.50 PMPM, per the DOJ complaint ([Lawyer Monthly](https://www.lawyer-monthly.com/2026/06/justice-department-sues-ppl-new-york-medicaid-fraud/)).
  - Wisconsin: realized $76.50 in 2025 ([DHS](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p03612-4q-25.pdf)); the 2026 contract rate is $82.77 ([contract](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/iris/cy2026-iris-fea-contract.pdf)).
  - Colorado: $103.21 for both Palco and PPL ([HCPF](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/sites/hcpf/files/HCPF%20OM%2024-039%20Consumer-Directed%20Attendant%20Support%20Services%20%28CDASS%29%20%20Changes%20to%20Per-Member-Per-Month%20%28PMPM%29%20Rates.pdf)†).
  - Texas: $114.40 for consumer-directed services and $210.08 for STAR+PLUS plans ([TCHP](https://www.texaschildrenshealthplan.org/news/provider-alert/hhsc-publishes-payment-rates-financial-management-services-agencies)†, [UHC](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/resource-library/news/2022/tx-star-plus-billing-change.html)†).
  - Louisiana: $105.88 ([memo](https://www.ldh.la.gov/assets/docs/OAAS/Support-Coordination-Memos/OAAS-SC-23-022-New-Service-SD-Financial-Management-Services-Admin-Fee-I-9-29-23.pdf), not re-verified).
  - PPL says pre-2025 New York fees ran $150-$1,050 ([PPL, self-interested](https://pplfirst.com/?p=20928)).
- **Pattern.** Competitive statewide awards price at $68-83. Only state rate-card or plan-paid programs reach $103-210.
- **Pool arithmetic (A).** 540,000 x $76-103 x 12 = $0.5-0.67B outside NY and CA. New York adds $0.17-0.21B (209,000-250,000 people at $68.50). The fee pool is **about $0.7-0.9B**, below the gate's $0.8-1.2B.
- **Headline contract values mislead.** Wisconsin's single-vendor contract is reported at $1.4B ([AOL/Center Square](https://www.aol.com/articles/questions-linger-wisconsin-medicaid-manager-160000138.html)). With 29,000 participants and $1.5B of 2026 cost ([WisPolitics](https://www.wispolitics.com/?p=419079)†), the vendor's fee is about $29M a year, roughly 2% (A). New York's roughly $9B program yields about $172-205M a year of fees (A), matching the "just over $1 billion over five years" report†.
- **Participants needed for $100M (A).** About 109,000 at $76.50, 101,000 at $82.77, or 81,000 at $103. That is **15-20% of the non-NY, non-CA pool**, or about half of New York's 209,000.
- **New York volume is unstable.** The state reported about 280,000 authorized before the switch, 209,000 registered with PPL by May 2025, and 75,000 moved to agency-based personal care ([NY DOH](https://healthweb-back.health.ny.gov/press/releases/2025/2025-05-19_cdpap_update.htm)). FI-served consumers fell about 25% in one rebid.

## 3. Competitors: confirmed, corrected, added

| **PPL** | Confirmed. Backed by DW Healthcare and Linden ([HHCN 2022](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2022/08/two-private-equity-firms-reportedly-back-self-directed-at-home-care-enabler-public-partnerships/)†). Sole New York FI since 2025-04-01. Wisconsin notice of intent in January 2026, three rivals protested, no contract signed ([Wisconsin Health News](https://wisconsinhealthnews.com/2026/07/16/legislators-question-dhs-over-plan-to-award-iris-contract/)). Sued by DOJ in E.D.N.Y. for a receiver; PPL's reply on its motion to dismiss was filed 2026-09-11 and I found no ruling ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2026/07/ppl-seeks-to-dismiss-ny-cdpap-case/), [docket](https://litigationtracker.law.georgetown.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Public-Partnerships_2026.09.11_DEFENDANT-PUBLIC-PARTNERSHIPS-REPLY-RE-MOTION-TO-DISMISS.pdf)†). |
| **GT Independence** | Confirmed but **corrected**: H.I.G. says "more than 50,000" people in 18 states plus DC, not the gate's 60,000+ ([H.I.G.](https://hig.com/news/h-i-g-capital-completes-significant-investment-in-gt-independence/)). H.I.G. manages $70B and invested in November 2025, so a funded roll-up competitor already exists. |
| **Acumen** | Confirmed. Alpine Investors-backed through TEAM Services Group ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/acumen-fiscal-agent)†). It left Colorado in April 2021 ([HCPF](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/sites/hcpf/files/CM%20FMS%20Workflow%20412021.pdf)†). |
| **Palco** | Confirmed. Won West Virginia statewide (4,900+ people) from PPL on 2024-04-01 ([BMS](https://bms.wv.gov/article/dohss-bureau-medical-services-selects-new-financial-management-services-vendor)). Self-reports 10,000+ participants ([Palco](https://www.palcofirst.com/?p=169)†). Plan-contracted statewide FI for Pennsylvania's managed-care waiver, on HHAX software ([HHAX](https://www.hhaexchange.com/press-releases/hhaexchange-and-tempus-unlimited-partner-self-direction-solution-for-pennsylvania)). Its 990 shows 2023 revenue of $1.99B, up from $634M in 2021 ([ProPublica](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/042239746)). |

| **Others** | Wisconsin's iLife, Premier and Outreach. Minnesota has 15 enrolled FMS providers ([MN DHS](https://mn.gov/dhs/disability-aging/home-and-community-services/programs-and-services/fms/)†). - **No venture-funded FMS startup found.** I ran five searches and did not verify two names from a 2026 opinion piece.
- **Substitutes.** The gate's "no free or in-house substitute" is only partly true. California runs its own payroll. Agency-with-choice is a recognized alternative model ([MACPAC](https://macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/03_February-Slides_Self-Direction-for-Home-and-Community-Based-Services-Key-actors-in-program-administration.pdf)). Minnesota is moving to a multi-vendor choice model.

## 4. Demand and willingness to pay

- **Mandated spend, state signer.** MACPAC lists FMS as a core function of self-direction, including EVV operation ([MACPAC](https://macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/03_February-Slides_Self-Direction-for-Home-and-Community-Based-Services-Key-actors-in-program-administration.pdf)). Signers are state Medicaid or developmental-disability directors, or plans in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Texas.
- **The procurement wave is real.**
  - New York: awarded 2024. Reportedly only 4 of 130+ bidders qualified ([City & State](https://www.cityandstateny.com/policy/2025/08/state-planned-give-no-bid-contract-ppl-lawmaker-claims/407621/)†).
  - West Virginia: 2024.
  - Wisconsin: three or four incumbent FEAs to one (press says three; the 2025 financials list four), start April 2027 ([AOL](https://www.aol.com/articles/questions-linger-wisconsin-medicaid-manager-160000138.html)).
  - Kentucky: RFP due 2026-11-06. The two listings carry conflicting dates and no participant count ([Govly](https://app.govly.com/public/opportunities/16859242)). I could not size it.
  - Ohio DODD: closed 2026-01-14, award not found ([SamSearch](https://samsearch.co/gov-explore/sled/ddd-statewide-financial-management-services-for-the-department-of-developmental/SRC0000028354)†).
- **But winners are incumbents with past performance.** The New York RFP required a statewide FI contract in another state as of 2024-04-01 and a **$100M line of credit** ([Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/11/cdpap-fiscal-intermediary-takes-aim-at-dohs-competitive)). It also required being in business before 2012 ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2024/09/competition-heats-up-for-new-york-cdpap-contract/)). In every award I found, the winner already held statewide FMS contracts elsewhere (PPL, Tempus, Palco); no company without that record won.
- **Payroll certainty is already a contract term, not a differentiator.** Wisconsin treats a missed payroll deadline as grounds for fiscal corrective action and can withhold or recover fee payments ([contract](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/iris/cy2026-iris-fea-contract.pdf)). Connecticut bills would add penalties for late payroll ([SB 487](https://prdext3.cga.ct.gov/2026/cbs/S/pdf/SB-0487.pdf); [SB 498 analysis](https://prdext2.cga.ct.gov/2026/ba/pdf/2026SB-00498-R000487-BA.pdf)†). Passage is not confirmed. The demand signal is real, but it makes the SLA table stakes.
- **Evidence that fees can move.** Wisconsin's 2026 rate is $82.77 against $76.50 realized in 2025, about +8% (A). Plans in New York dispute PPL's request for $0.55 more per hour ([Spectrum](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2025/12/11/n-y--health-plans-accuse-medicaid-home-care-company-of-violating-antitrust-laws)).

## 5. Unit economics and capital

**Wisconsin FEAs, the best hard analog** ([2025](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p03612-4q-25.pdf), [2024](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p03612-4q-24.pdf)). Dollars are per participant per month.

| FEA | 2025 revenue | 2025 operating cost | 2025 net | 2024 net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GT Independence (about 8,500 people) | $77.47 | $76.02 | +$1.46 | +$5.00 |
| iLife | $75.73 | $85.40 | -$9.67 | -$13.33 |
| Premier | $77.84 | $103.34 | -$25.51 | -$21.18 |
| Outreach | $76.12 | $94.39 | -$38.41 | +$1.99 |
| **All four (about 27,700 people)** | **$76.50** | **$84.87** | **-$9.53 (-12.5%)** | **-$9.03 (-11.8%)** |

- **Implication.** The best operators' cost ($71-76) leaves about 2-7% margin at $77. iLife, the largest at about 14,800 people, costs more per head than GT at about 8,500, so scale alone did not lower cost. A 10-15% margin at $76-83 requires cost of about $65-75. Only the two best Wisconsin results in 2024 ($71) fall inside that range, and only at the $83 price. New York's $68.50 is under the best Wisconsin cost. That implies either large scale economies or under-costing; DOJ alleges PPL misrepresented its costs (unproven).
- **Tempus** earned about $7.9M on $1.99B in 2023 (0.4%) with $23M of staff wages ([ProPublica](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/042239746)). It is a nonprofit, so this is not a margin analog.
- **Regulatory capital is small.** Wisconsin requires working capital of at least 2% of revenue plus a restricted reserve at 8%, 4%, 3%, 2% and 1% across revenue tiers ([contract](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/iris/cy2026-iris-fea-contract.pdf)). At $100M revenue that is about $4M (A). It also requires $1M general and professional liability, D&O, umbrella and a fidelity bond.
- **Payroll float is the real capital need.** New York's roughly $36k per participant (A) implies about $59M a week for 85,000 people. A two-week backstop is about $120M, consistent with the $100M line New York demanded. PPL paid more than $240M in its first April weeks ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/04/new-york-consumers-home-care-workers-protest-cdpap/)†). I found no sourced commitment-fee pricing.
- **Acquisition cost.** I found no prices for any FMS deal; H.I.G.'s GT terms were undisclosed.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **Tax.** An IRS Section 3504 agent is jointly and severally liable with each employer for employment taxes and penalties, using Form 2678 ([IRS](https://www.irs.gov/government-entities/federal-state-local-governments/third-party-payer-arrangements-section-3504-agents)). The FI carries every participant-employer's tax risk.
- **Wage-hour.** Joint-employer status is contested. Talarico v. PPL went against PPL in the Third Circuit in 2020 and for PPL in an unpublished May 2026 opinion ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/ip-law/home-care-workers-fail-in-joint-employer-unpaid-overtime-appeal)†). New York's Calderon class action settled for **$162M** ([Legal Aid](https://legalaidnyc.org/court-case/philip-calderon-v-public-partnerships-llc/)†). That is about 79-94% of one year of New York fee revenue (A). One report breaks it into $92M unused vacation, $40.5M general damages and $25M health insurance†.
- **Fraud.** DOJ seeks a receiver under 18 U.S.C. 1345. Wisconsin can suspend fee payments on a credible fraud allegation (42 CFR 455.23). CMS named personal care and HCBS for scrutiny in February 2026 ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2026/02/cms-targets-medicaid-personal-care-hcbs-in-sweeping-fraud-crackdown/)). All 48 responding states cross-check claims to EVV, and 21 use or plan AI ([KFF via HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2026/10/states-go-beyond-federal-requirements-to-fight-medicaid-home-care-fraud/)).
- **Political.** New York bills would restore multiple FIs; passage not confirmed ([HHCN](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2025/05/new-york-lawmakers-introduce-bill-to-reverse-cdpap-changes/)†). Wisconsin legislators want the PPL award paused. The single-vendor model is now politically contested, which cuts both ways for a challenger.

## 7. Is the why-now real?

Partly. Consolidation procurements are live, and New York cut its fee from a reported $150-$1,000+ to $68.50 (state and PPL figures, unaudited). But New York's day-one payroll failures, the DOJ suit and the settlement now make states cautious about single vendors and about new entrants. The $100M prize is a five-year contract from April 2025† with no rebid scheduled. A new New York slot needs a receivership or legislative reversal, both speculative.

## 8. Upside-case assumptions tested

| Assumption | Evidence | Holds? |
|---|---|---|
| About $100 blended PMPM | Contested statewide awards run $68.50-82.77. Only rate-card states reach $103+. | **No.** Use $75-85. |
| About 85,000 participants | 1.7x GT's 50,000 after 21 years. At $80 you need about 104,000 (A). | **Heroic.** |
| 10-15% margin | Sector margin -12% in Wisconsin. Best operator +2% to +6.5%. | **No evidence.** |
| 30-40% of timesheets need a human | No public rejection rate found. Connecticut bills ask states to collect one. | **Unsourced.** |
| "EVV equals timesheet" as a wedge | Vendor feature at HHAX; DCI and CYMA handle FI payroll. | **Not unique.** |
| Buy a small FI for past performance | Matches New York's qualifier. But H.I.G. and Alpine are buyers, and Wisconsin's losers (iLife, Premier, Outreach) lose money. | **Plausible, contested.** |
| Kentucky and Ohio as wedges | Kentucky size unknown. At $100 PMPM, 4,900 people (West Virginia) is about $5.9M a year (A). | **Wedge is $5-30M.** |
| MCO-delegated second channel | Real: Pennsylvania plans, Horizon NJ, Texas plans. But New York plans are fighting PPL on rates. | **Real, price-contested.** |

## 9. Synthesis

**Moats.**
- Switching costs: **Moderate.** States do switch (West Virginia from PPL to Palco, Pennsylvania's managed-care waiver from PPL to Tempus in 2022 ([PA providers](https://www.paproviders.org/?p=25195)†), Colorado after Acumen left).
- Scale economies: **Unproven** below 30,000 people; New York's $68.50 suggests they exist at 200,000+, but that is unaudited.
- Intangibles (past performance, state certification): **Moderate**, and held by incumbents.
- Network effects: **None.**

**Scenarios (A, my judgment).**

| Scenario | Probability | Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Bull | 10% | A New York receivership or rebid, or two or three large state consolidations, gives $100M+ revenue. |
| Base | 50% | Acquire a small FI and win one or two mid-size states: $15-35M revenue at 0-6% margin. |
| Bear | 40% | Lose rebids to PPL, Tempus or Palco, or get outbid for targets by H.I.G.: $5-10M, thin. |

**Under the lessons filter:** the payer and budget line are real, and the legal premise is checked. Fails the hidden-incumbent test (funded consolidators already exist) and the fee is too thin to pay for a guaranteed-payroll SLA. Lesson 7 applies. The gate already shrank the idea from "30% under" to an SLA, and the SLA is a contract term.

**Cheap tests before any commitment.**
1. Obtain Wisconsin's RFP price scoring and the protest outcome.
2. Get Kentucky's participant count.
3. Ask two FI operators for cost per participant-month at 10,000 and 50,000 people.
4. Wait for the E.D.N.Y. ruling on the receiver request.

**Gaps.** No FMS deal prices. No vendor margins outside Wisconsin. No Ohio or Kentucky awards or sizes. No rejection-rate data. The Wisconsin award outcome is unknown.

ideas.title: Large-Load Queue Bureau: reality scores that price the $50,000-per-MW deposit
ideas.one_liner: A furnisher-funded bureau that sees the same data-center project in every utility and ISO queue, scores how much of each megawatt is physically real, and uses that score to verify applicants for grid operators and to underwrite the interconnection deposits that now forfeit 80% if a project falls out.
ideas.customer: Three buyers on one dataset: (1) grid operators and utilities running large-load queues (ERCOT first, then other RTOs/ISOs, which FERC's June 18, 2026 show-cause orders put under pressure, and utilities with 1 GW+ queues); (2) data-center and powered-land developers who must post security, especially non-investment-grade neoclouds and landowners; (3) private-credit and infrastructure funds, lenders and insurers that fund deposits or lend against sites and GPUs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Bureau: Director/VP of Large Load Interconnection or Transmission Planning at a utility, or the grid-planning VP at an ISO, funded from interconnection study-fee revenue and planning budgets; applicants (developer CFO or head of power) pay a per-application verified-ready fee. Credit layer: developer CFO signs the credit-support fee; an infrastructure-credit fund MD signs the capital. Budget line exists: Texas Batch Zero requires $50,000/MW of security (about $9.7B ceiling across about 194 GW conditionally classified, my arithmetic from ERCOT figures via search summaries) and ERCOT/PUCT are running a mandated verification and audit.
ideas.problem: Each queue sees only its own entries, so one project shopped to several utilities is counted several times. ERCOT tracks about 474 GW of large-load requests, about 90% data centers. Texas now prices phantom load: SB 6 (75 MW+) and the PUCT-approved Batch Zero rule require proof of site control and $50,000/MW security (cash, investment-grade guaranty, or A-/A3 bank letter of credit), with 20% refunded and 80% forfeited to the transmission provider's rate base if a load withdraws or misses a milestone by six months (refundability rules were reportedly still not formally adopted at the July 10 deposit deadline). Governor Abbott's Aug 3, 2026 directive has ERCOT auditing roughly 250-300 projects / about 200 GW by December 2026, by hand, queue by queue. Developers without rated balance sheets cannot post the security, and the only dedicated funder found is a $95M two-site fund.
ideas.solution: 1) Per-project evidence file from the public trail (recorded deeds/options/memoranda, rezoning agendas, air permits and generator counts, water filings, tax abatements, LLC and principal cross-matching, equipment lead-time feasibility) scored into probability-weighted realized MW with confidence bands. 2) A cross-queue duplicate registry: utilities and ISOs contribute hashed site/principal identifiers and get duplicate flags and scores back (the credit-bureau furnish-to-receive model). 3) A verified-ready attestation applicants hand to an ISO in response to an RFI. 4) A credit layer that uses the score and realized/withdrawn outcome history to underwrite and arrange deposit funding from infrastructure-credit capital, starting as underwriter/sub-adviser to a licensed manager rather than on own balance sheet.
ideas.why_now: PUCT approved Batch Zero on June 18, 2026; deposits were due July 10; Abbott ordered the verification audit on Aug 3, with completion targeted for December 2026 and MW allocations due April 9, 2027; FERC issued show-cause orders to all six RTOs/ISOs on June 18, 2026 naming speculative or duplicative requests; ERCOT conditionally classified 362 projects / about 194 GW in September. For the first time every queue entry has a price, a forfeiture rule and a regulator asking whether it is real, and other states and RTOs are likely to copy the design.
ideas.wedge: Texas: the 362 Batch Zero projects. Sell fixed-fee public-trail evidence files ($15-40K) to (a) deposit funders and lenders who need underwriting, (b) developers who must answer ERCOT RFIs, and (c) the round-1 channel, intervenor groups funding docket audits ($40-120K). Use that revenue to build the scored dataset, then pitch a hashed duplicate-check pilot to one utility planning group and ERCOT.
ideas.path_to_100m: Data/verification layer (all counts and prices are my assumptions): 7 ISOs/RTOs x $2M = $14M; 100 utilities with 1 GW+ queues x $400K = $40M; 2,000 applications a year x $15-20K = $30-40M; 150 lender/insurer/fund seats x $100K = $15M. That sums to about $100M at 100% penetration, so a realistic 50-60% is $50-65M. Credit layer: if 20-30% of the ERCOT ceiling needs third-party funding ($1.9-2.9B per cycle) and platform economics are 4-5% over about two years, the whole pool is $80-145M per cycle and a 20% share is $16-29M, requiring repeated batches plus 2-3 other markets copying the rule. ideas.who_does_it_today: ERCOT, PUCT and transmission-provider staff run RFIs and the audit manually, per queue; I found no cross-utility registry. Market-intelligence vendors sell to developers and investors: Enverus (publishes Batch Zero readiness analysis; page would not open), Cleanview, SynMax Vulcan, Epoch AI hub. Deposit finance: Dynamix Capital Partners / Staubach Capital / Soda Springs 'SSSC Batch Zero Fund', $95M, about 1.7 GW across two Texas sites (single trade source, no fee or return disclosed); banks supply letters of credit to rated names. ideas.why_they_lose: Consultancies see one client's queue and are conflicted when the audit target is their own client. ideas.customer: State human-services agencies in the 41 states plus DC that were above the 6% SNAP error threshold in FY2025, starting with states in the 8-13% error band with system releases due Oct 2026-Jan 2027; later their Medicaid eligibility agencies.

ideas.problem: Under H.R.1, from FY2028 (Oct 1, 2027) states pay 5%, 10% or 15% of SNAP benefit costs when their payment error rate is 6-8%, 8-10% or over 10%. The FY2025 national rate was 10.62% (about $10.1B improper payments; 41 states plus DC above 6%). For FY2028 a state may use its FY2025 or FY2026 rate; from FY2029 the rate from three years earlier applies, so FY2027, which began Oct 1, 2026, sets FY2030. The most expensive error is one the system makes identically thousands of times (round-1 file cites a North Carolina shelter-deduction bug fixed by a one-click prompt used more than 20,000 times). Vendors test their own work and states lack independent boundary-case test data with signed-off answers. Admin cost share also moves to 75% state from FY2027 (round-1 file, not re-verified), and Medicaid work requirements start Jan 1, 2027 in 43 states.
ideas.solution: Three layers sold as one program. 1) H.R.1 conformance packs: about 250 synthetic households per rule change with state-signed expected outcomes, run in the state's UAT (the round-1 product). 2) Weekly re-adjudication of a statistically valid sample of the state's own closed cases against the answer key using a rules engine plus an LLM, predicting what federal QC will find and root-causing by rule, system module and office. 3) A fix loop: system change tickets with test evidence plus worker drills generated from the same answer-key corpus. Price: fixed fee for layers 1-2 plus a gainshare on the cost-share tier avoided.
ideas.why_now: USDA released FY2025 error rates on June 24, 2026; FY2028 cost-share starts in 12 months; the FY2027 rate (current year) sets FY2030; states are already appropriating (Florida $4M) and procuring AI vendors; Medicaid and SNAP rule reprogramming is landing at once around Jan 2027; and the answer key is exactly what an auditor of last resort needs when a state's QC is checked by USDA.
ideas.wedge: Sell the H.R.1 Conformance Pack at $40-120K per rule change to 2-3 states whose SNAP system releases are due Oct 2026-Jan 2027 and that already run UAT, with a free QC-risk memo on state policy versus federal guidance as the door-opener. ideas.path_to_100m: Fixed-fee path: 41 states x $2.5-4M (assumption; Florida's $4M is the only anchor) = $105-165M for SNAP alone, so $100M would need most of the pool; not credible alone. Gainshare path: moving California from the 15% to the 10% tier avoids about $630M a year (derived from CBPP's $1.9B x 5/15), Florida about $330M, Texas from 10% to 5% $375M (sourced). That is roughly $1.3B a year across three states, and a 5% gainshare is about $65M. Add 5-7 mid-size states at $100-300M avoided each and the total is $90-140M. This needs three unproven things: the tooling cuts error rates by 2-4 points; states may legally pay gainshare (federal cost-allowability and state procurement rules, unverified); and you win 8-10 large-state procurements of 12-18 months each. Heroic share and the weakest of the two ideas on the $100M bar.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Maximus 'Accuracy Assistant', a SNAP-specific suite using predictive analytics to flag inconsistencies, which works inside live cases; Maximus calls SNAP an emerging opportunity and described an expanded role with an unnamed long-time state customer. The integrators that build and maintain eligibility systems (Deloitte, Accenture, Gainwell, Conduent, Tyler and others); searches found no SNAP error-reduction award for Deloitte or Conduent, which proves little. Code for America and PolicyEngine (nonprofit and open-source rules engine). Florida's selected AI vendor (unnamed; no award found). Round 1's competitor check for this idea was partial and found no startup. On the Medicaid side, most states say they will use incumbent vendors and CMS negotiated discounted vendor rates, so that side is harder to enter.
ideas.why_they_lose: Integrators build the logic that causes systematic errors and earn on change orders, so they cannot sell independence. Maximus assists workers in live cases rather than testing the system against an independent state-signed answer key. Time-and-materials contractors cannot copy an outcome price without cannibalizing themselves.
